answer.rationale: The mandate (18% cut) plus the incumbent's refusal to reopen price plus a contract that lapses in 14 days effectively eliminates renew_incumbent and defer_decision as sufficient answers, and negotiate_terms (memory_c4, memory_c6) is already foreclosed this cycle by the refusal. That leaves the low-cost vendor, which means the entire decision rests on memory_c2 — the single most load-bearing inherited claim and the one whose failure mode is most expensive. So memory_c2 is the memory worth my one verification pull. What I need from the archive is not the summary conclusion but its scope: 'last year' at what volume, what part numbers, and whether 'onboarding was quick' was measured against a line running with slack rather than at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. A cost-and-invoicing result observed at low volume with buffer does not transfer cleanly to a full-rate migration with no recovery room; the consolidated note has been compressed to its favorable outcome and the qualifying conditions may have been dropped in consolidation. I therefore intend to switch primary supply but to execute it as a phased migration rather than a single cutover: move a defined tranche of volume to the low-cost vendor while bridging remaining volume on month-to-month terms (the mechanism memory_c5 shows is available), so the 94% utilization constraint is not exposed to a cold-start ramp. This deliberately captures less of the quoted savings than a clean switch would, which is the price of not betting an unbuffered line on an unverified transfer. Downstream risk I am flagging explicitly: at 94% commitment, any early-life quality or ramp shortfall at the new vendor converts directly into missed committed volume with no catch-up capacity, and memory_c3's dual-source lesson — that removing the single point of failure is what held allocation through a shortage — argues against replacing one sole-source dependency with a different sole-source dependency. If verification shows memory_c2's result came from a materially smaller or non-critical volume, I will de-scope the first tranche further and treat this as qualification rather than migration; if it shows comparable full-rate volume, I will widen the tranche. Either way I am not resolving the tension between the cost mandate and the zero-buffer line this cycle, only sequencing it, and the second-source question stays open for the next review.
